title: Dolly Parton graces the college football landscape on season’s first full Saturday
content:
The calendar read 9/5, and across college football, Dolly Parton seemed to be everywhere. Her songs floated from stadium speakers, her butterfly flashed on uniforms and helmets, and the sport’s familiar Saturday pageantry made room for one long, scattered tribute.

College football Saturdays run on repetition, with the same soundtrack, symbols and rituals repeated so faithfully that generations of fans know the cues. On Saturday, that language bent toward Parton — nowhere more naturally than in Tennessee.

All afternoon, Parton’s butterfly seemed to grow. It began on the backs of Tennessee’s helmets as an orange-and-white decal bearing her name as part of a season-long tribute. But by halftime, the image escaped those few inches as the Pride of the Southland Band gave Parton’s most enduring symbol a much larger stage.

As the band moved through “9 to 5” and “I Will Always Love You,” Neyland’s turf became something closer to stationery. Musicians traced Parton’s looping signature across the field, then rearranged themselves into a butterfly. Her handwriting and symbol were briefly rendered at football-field scale.

But the most affecting moment, perhaps, came only after the band had packed away the spectacle.

During a break in the action on the field, the opening notes of “I Will Always Love You” came over the stadium speakers as part of a Dolly-themed karaoke segment. It swelled into more than 100,000 voices, as the chorus rose from every tier and moved through the stadium on its own.

Parton became a refrain Saturday. “Jolene” accompanied the spirit squad onto the field. Singing fans flashed across the videoboards on the “Dolly Karaoke Cam.” And when the fourth quarter arrived, even one of Neyland’s oldest game-day cues yielded to Parton: “My Tennessee Mountain Home” replaced the Vols’ customary song.

By then, the tribute no longer felt like a single planned ceremony. Parton was threaded into the rhythm of the game — tucked onto helmets, written across the field and sung during stoppages.

It was a fitting setting. Parton’s roots run through East Tennessee and into the university itself: UT awarded her an honorary doctorate in 2009, and in 2023 she returned to the stadium to sing “Rocky Top” alongside Peyton Manning before a game against Georgia.

This time, Neyland did the singing for her.

About 180 miles west in Murfreesboro, Middle Tennessee’s tribute carried an almost too-perfect coincidence: its season opener against Murray State fell on 9/5.

The Blue Raiders marked the date by wearing a commemorative patch featuring Parton’s signature, a butterfly and the years “1946-2026,” a nod made all the more fitting by Saturday’s date and one of the songs most inseparable from Parton’s legendary career.

QR codes on the Floyd Stadium scoreboard directed fans to donate to Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library, the book-gifting program she founded in 1995 that grew into one of the most visible parts of her philanthropic legacy.

Middle Tennessee also plans to preserve part of the tribute. The first game-worn jersey featuring the patch is set to be donated to the university’s Center for Popular Music, where it will join a collection devoted to American music history.

Parton’s Saturday footprint stretched improbably west, all the way to Eugene, Oregon. There, nearly 2,500 miles from Knoxville, college football had long ago adopted one of her songs as its own.

Before Oregon hosted Boise State at Autzen Stadium, the Ducks played a tribute video to Parton set to “Eugene, Oregon,” the song she wrote after visiting the city in 1972. A green-and-yellow butterfly filled the video board, displaying one of Parton’s most recognizable symbols with the school’s colors.

Outside Eugene, “Eugene, Oregon” is a deep cut. Inside Autzen, it’s become a victory song. Oregon plays it after Ducks wins, giving one of Parton’s lesser-known tracks a second life in the place that first inspired it.

The first full Saturday of college football usually announces new beginnings. This one kept finding ways to remember what had been lost.
